TESSERACT,
by 26855.

Our robot is built from several connected systems, and each one helps the team move, collect, score, and compete.

See how our bot works on the field

Our robot, Tesseract, is unique in both functionality and design. Its custom two launcer system allows it to maximize efficiency and overall success on the field. It is capable of scoring quickly and consistently, while still sorting artifacts by color.

Subsystems that make the bot compete

Drivetrain & chassis

The chassis is made of two pairs of c-channels forming parallel tubes. These tubes hold the drive motors, holding them perpendicular to the drive axels. The wheels and the motors are connected with 90 degree gear boxes. To drive, the bot uses omnidirectional mechanum wheels. To prevent tipping, steel ball transfers are located on all four corners.

Intake

The intake uses custom made silicon wheels. These wheels pull the artifacts up a 3d printed ramp. The ramp takes up the entire front side of the bot to maximize the efficiency of the intake.

Sorter

Once the artifacts are pulled up the ramp, they are sorted by color sensors on each side of the bot.

Aiming

The bot uses a combination of AprilTag detection (with a camera), dead wheel tracking, and IMU (inertial measurement unit), to track the goal down to plus or minus 2 inches and 0.5 degrees and automatically aims towards the goal.

Double launcher innovation

Initial Innovation

At the beginning of the season, we sat down and discussed what the most overall effective system would be. We initially decided that being able to launch 3 artifacts would be the optimal strategy. It would allow for an option between speed and sorting. We were aware that a system like this would be unique and present several challenges, but decided that the benefit would outweigh the costs.

Initial Roadblocks and Fixes

As soon as we started prototyping a three ball launcher, we realized that size would be an issue. The launchers had to fit within 18 inches, and 3 artifacts lined up was already 15 inches. We eventually decided that a three launcher system was not feasible, but that a two launcher system would still benefit us immensely.

The First Attempt

Before our first league meet, we were able to assemble a functional prototype of the double launcher. This prototype used two pairs of flywheels rotating the artifacts around a ramp constructed out of sheet metal and cardboard. This competition went quite poorly. While the bot was able to launch artifacts very quickly, accuracy suffered severely. It was after this that we realized that, in order to ensure accuracy, we needed to use rails manufactured out of PLA+ instead of ramps. Rails make sure that the artifacts’ path moves on a plane perfectly perpendicular to the front of the bot.

The Final Design

Our current launcher uses a refined version of the original rails that we manufactured. They are held together in four separate spots to maintain consistent compression throughout the entire launch sequence. They were also designed to be highly adjustable, allowing them to adapt to any changes that might be made to the bot. The pairs of flywheels are separated by 3d printed spacers that also serve as inertial batteries. These batteries contain weights. This increases the axles inertia, stopping the flywheels from loosing speed as artifacts pass through them. All of these features working together result in a unique and Innovative robot that has the capability to both score artifacts in an extremely quick manner while still being able to sort balls by color. This gives us the best strategic balance between the Goal and Pattern ranking point.

Our build journey

1

Define the issue at hand by framing it in the format of “We are solving [issue] because [reason the issue needs to be solved]."

→
2

Have a whole team meeting to brainstorm possible solutions. Everyone has to contribute an idea no matter how silly it is, because sometimes those are the most innovative.

→
3

Create a pros and cons list for each idea, then hold a vote to decide which idea/ideas we are going to try (usually we end up with 2-3 that wetry).

4

Assign small groups to prototype each of the ideas chosen in step 3.

→
5

Test all the prototypes and vote on which one is the most effective in fulfilling the statement from step 1.

→
6

Design, test, and install the the decided idea. If it doesn’t end up working, return to step 5.
